newsitem.title: USA: FULL TEXT - Intel Q2 results.
newsitem.headline: FULL TEXT - Intel Q2 results.

text.p: Intel Corp Tuesday reported second quarter results slightly ahead of Wall Street's expectations. The following is a copy of Intel's news release.

SANTA CLARA, Calif., July 15, 1997--Intel's newest processors, the Pentium(R) processor with MMX(TM) technology and the Pentium(R) II processor, experienced rapid market acceptance in the second quarter, the company said today.

However, revenue and earnings in the seasonally slower second quarter were down from the first quarter due to a combination of weakness in Europe, an inventory correction following a strong first quarter and product transitions in the PC industry.
Second quarter revenue was $6.0 billion, up 29 percent from $4.6 billion for the second quarter of 1996. Second quarter revenue was down 7.6 percent from first quarter 1997 revenue of $6.4 billion.
Net income in the second quarter was $1.6 billion, up 58 percent from second quarter 1996 net income of $1.0 billion, and down 17 percent from first quarter 1997 net income of $2.0 billion.

Earnings per share in the second quarter rose to $0.92 from $0.59 in the second quarter of 1996, an increase of 56 percent. Earnings per share in the second quarter dropped 16 percent from $1.10 in the first quarter of 1997.
All of the share and per-share amounts in this release have been adjusted to reflect a 2-for-1 stock distribution that was paid July 13, 1997 to stockholders of record on June 10, 1997.

"Strong microprocessor shipments in the first quarter led to some inventory correction in the second quarter as the industry prepared for a rapid transition to processors with MMX technology," said Dr. Andrew S. Grove, chairman and chief executive officer. "Demand for the Pentium processor with MMX technology and the Pentium II processor is strong, and we are ramping production at a record rate."

In the second quarter, the company repurchased a total of 13.0 million shares of Common Stock at a cost of $945 million under an ongoing program. Since the program began in 1990, the company has repurchased 198.2 million shares at a total cost of $5.6 billion.

During the quarter, Intel's Board of Directors declared a $0.03 per share quarterly dividend, an increase of 20 percent from the previous per share quarterly dividend. The dividend is payable on September 1, 1997 to stockholders of record on August 1, 1997. Upon payment of this dividend, Intel will have paid a quarterly dividend for the past five years.

The following statements are based on current expectations. These statements are forward looking and actual results may differ materially. -0- -- The company expects revenue for the third quarter of 1997 to be flat to slightly up from second quarter revenue of $6.0 billion. -- Gross margin percentage in the third quarter of 1997 is expected to be flat to slightly down from 61 percent in the second quarter. Intel's gross margin expectation for 1997 is 60 percent plus or minus a few points. Based on first half of 1997 results and current expectations, gross margin percentage for 1997 is expected to be at the mid to high part of that range. In the short-term Intel's gross margin percentage varies primarily with revenue levels and product mix. -- The company still believes that over the long-term the gross margin percentage will be 50 percent plus or minus a few points. Intel's long-term gross margin percentage will vary depending on product mix. -- Expenses (R & D plus MG &A) in the third quarter of 1997 are expected to be approximately 4 to 6 percent higher than expenses of $1.3 billion in the second quarter, subject in part to revenue dependent expenses. -- R & D spending for 1997 is expected to be approximately $2.4 billion. -- The tax rate in 1997 is expected to remain at 35.5 percent. -- The company expects interest and other income for the third quarter of 1997 to be approximately $140 million, assuming no significant changes in cash balances or interest rates and no unanticipated items. -- Capital spending is expected to be approximately $4.5 billion in 1997. Depreciation is expected to be approximately $560 million for the third quarter and $2.2 billion for 1997, down from previous guidance of approximately $2.5 billion.

The above statements contained in this outlook are forward-looking statements that involve a number of risks and uncertainties. In addition to the factors discussed above, among the other factors that could cause actual results to differ materially are the following: business conditions and growth in the computing industry and in the general economy; changes in customer order patterns, including timing of delivery and changes in seasonal fluctuations in PC buying patterns; competitive factors, such as rival chip architectures, competing software-compatible microprocessors, acceptance of new products and response to price pressures; unanticipated costs or other adverse effects associated with processors and other products containing errata (deviations from published specifications); risk of inventory obsolescence due to shifts in market demand; variations in inventory valuation; excess or shortage of purchased components; timing of software industry product introductions; continued success in technological advances and their implementation, including the manufacturing ramp; excess or shortage of manufacturing capacity; development, implementation and initial production of new strategic products and processes; risks associated with foreign operations; changes in the mixes of microprocessor types and speeds, motherboards, purchased components and other products; litigation involving intellectual property and consumer issues; level of stock repurchases; and other risk factors listed from time to time in the company's SEC reports, including but not limited to the report on Form 10-Q for the quarter ended March 29, 1997 (Part I, Item 2, Outlook section).

Unit shipments of microprocessors and chipsets were down in the second quarter from the first quarter of 1997. -- Motherboard units shipped in the second quarter were down from the first quarter of 1997, however motherboard units for the Pentium II processor were higher. -- Flash memory units shipped during the quarter set a record. -- Embedded processor and microcontroller units shipped were flat with the first quarter. -- Revenue from networking products increased in the second quarter from the first quarter. Units of fast ethernet network interface cards and hubs were up in the second quarter from the first quarter. -- Gross margin percentage declined in the second quarter from the first quarter of 1997, primarily as a consequence of lower sequential revenues with fixed depreciation and other non-variable costs. Also contributing to lower gross margin percentage was slightly higher than normal inventory write-offs. -- Intel's revenue breakdown by major geographic regions is summarized below:
-- Japan and Americas regions had sequentially higher revenues in Q2. The combination of seasonally lower demand and an inventory correction in Europe led to lower sequential revenue in that region.
-- Employment at the end of the second quarter of 1997 was 57,000, up from 52,000 at the end of the first quarter.

-- In May, the company introduced the Pentium II processor which provides the highest performance across the three vectors of performance, integer, floating point and multimedia, on the Intel architecture. The Pentium II processor uses the Dual Independent Bus architecture to provide up to three times the performance in processor-to-memory bandwidth as the single-bus, socket-7 generation processors such as the Pentium processor. The Pentium II processor combines the advanced technologies of the Pentium Pro processor with the capabilities of Intels MMX media enhancement technology. The Pentium II processor was introduced at speeds of 300, 266 and 233 MHz.

-- Intel introduced the 233-MHz Pentium processor with MMX technology, a new high performance processor for mainstream consumer PCs that run applications designed for Intels MMX media enhancement technology.
-- Intel expanded its line of mobile processors with MMX media enhancement technology. Intel now offers 166-, 150- and 133-MHz versions of its Pentium processor with MMX technology for notebooks.

-- During the quarter Intel and other industry leaders formally unveiled the Network PC (Net PC), a business PC designed specifically to help reduce PC support costs. The Net PC's advanced management technologies enable enhanced services such as remote system configuration, software installations and upgrades, off-hours maintenance, problem resolution and asset management.
-- Intel introduced the industry's first sub $100 per port 10/100Mbps stackable and manageable hub. Each Intel Express 10/100 Stackable Hub can operate at either 10 or 100 megabits-per-second (Mbps).

-- Intel introduced the 82558, the industry's first single-chip Fast Ethernet solution for networking at speeds of 10 or 100 Mbps. The 82558 supports three key capabilities required by the Wired for Management Baseline and Net PC specifications for remotely managing PCs via the LAN, including the Advanced Configuration and Power Interface, Wake-on-LAN and remote boot functionality.

-- Intel introduced the TeamStation(TM) System, a PC-based videoconferencing product that expands the communications capabilities for work being conducted in conference room environments. The TeamStation system includes video/audio/data conferencing and presentation capabilities, plus Internet and corporate network access.

-- Intel and Hewlett Packard announced that they plan to team up to offer quick and easy image capture, editing and publishing capabilities for home and business consumers. The two companies plan to work together to advance PC imaging industry specifications such as USB, Flash Memory Miniature Card, FlashPix(a) and MMX technology.
-- During the quarter, the company began shipping a mobile version of the Pentium processor with MMX technology, Intel's first product manufactured on 0.25 micron technology.
Q2 1997 net revenue of $6.0 billion was up 29 percent from Q2 1996 revenue of $4.6 billion, driven primarily by higher revenue from sales of processors and chipsets.
Revenue for the first six months of 1997 was $12.4 billion, up 34 percent from $9.3 billion in the first half of 1996.

Gross margin percentage in the second quarter was 61 percent, compared to 53 percent in the second quarter of 1996. The rise in the gross margin percentage was primarily the result of a more favorable product mix in Q2 1997.

Q2 1997 total expenses (R&D and MG&A) of $1.3 billion increased 34 percent from Q2 1996 expenses of $956 million due primarily to higher levels of R&D, advertising and revenue dependent expenses, such as Intel Inside spending. Expenses were 21 percent of revenues in Q2 1997, the same as in Q2 1996.
During the quarter, interest and other income was $212 million, up from $86 million in Q2 1996 due primarily to higher cash balances and gains on the sale of certain equity investments.

Capital spending was $969 million and depreciation was $529 million in Q2 1997. Accounts receivable decreased by $34 million in the quarter. The company's average days-sales-outstanding was 47, an increase of 3 days from the first quarter of 1997.

During Q2 1997, the company repurchased 13.0 million shares of common stock at a cost of $945 million under an ongoing program. As of June 28, 1997 the company's potential put warrant obligation was $1.6 billion to buy back 21.0 million shares of common stock. Of the total 280 million shares now authorized for repurchase, approximately 198.2 million shares have been repurchased and 60.8 million shares of common stock remain available for repurchase under the stock repurchase program, after reserving for 21.0 million shares to cover outstanding put warrants.
